The Cuban
Missile Crisis

13 Days That Changed the World
Defense Readiness Condition
DEFCON 5  ·  Peacetime

In October 1962, the United States and Soviet Union came closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history. For thirteen days, decisions made by three men, and one Soviet naval officer 300 feet underwater, determined the fate of the world.

Cuba
Soviet Missile Buildup

Beginning in the summer of 1962, the Soviet Union secretly shipped medium and intermediate-range ballistic missiles to Cuba. The operation, code-named Anadyr, involved over 40,000 Soviet military personnel.

U-2 reconnaissance aircraft. These spy planes discovered the missiles.

On October 14, Major Richard Heyser flew a U-2 mission over western Cuba. CIA analysts spent two days confirming what they saw before briefing the President on October 16.

MRBM Launch Site 1, San Cristobal, Cuba. October 23, 1962.
Missiles in Cuba could reach Washington D.C. in under 13 minutes.
Washington D.C.
The ExComm

On October 16, Kennedy secretly assembled the Executive Committee of the National Security Council, 13 advisors known as ExComm. For nearly two weeks they met in secret while Kennedy maintained his normal public schedule to avoid panic.

  • Do nothing, rejected as politically impossible
  • Diplomatic pressure only, seen as too weak
  • Naval blockade of Cuba
  • Air strikes and invasion, pushed hard by the Joint Chiefs

Kennedy chose the quarantine, buying time for diplomacy while keeping military options open.

The Atlantic
B-59 and the Soviet Submarines

Four Soviet submarines were running submerged toward Cuba, armed with nuclear torpedoes. They had been out of contact for weeks. Submarine B-59 would become the most dangerous vessel in history.

The crew believed nuclear war may have already begun above them.

The Quarantine Line
Naval Blockade

On October 24, Kennedy announced a naval quarantine, a blockade line 500 miles from Cuba. He chose the word deliberately. A "blockade" is an act of war under international law.

As US destroyers enforced the line, twenty Soviet vessels stopped and turned around. Secretary of State Rusk said: "We are eyeball to eyeball, and I think the other fellow just blinked."

Florida
Invasion Force

Approximately 180,000 troops were staged in Florida, ready to invade Cuba. This is critical context for the B-59 story. The Soviet crew, unable to receive communications and hearing depth charges, had every reason to believe the invasion had already begun.

Turkey
The Hidden Piece

Since 1961, the US had deployed Jupiter intermediate-range ballistic missiles in Turkey, pointed at the Soviet Union. Khrushchev publicly demanded their removal. Kennedy refused publicly. The secret: he privately agreed to remove them within six months. This was kept classified for decades.

A U.S. Air Force Jupiter IRBM. These missiles in Turkey were the hidden piece of the deal.
Soviet Union
The Supply Fleet

The Soviet operation to arm Cuba required a massive covert shipping operation. Cargo ships loaded weapons and personnel at ports in the Black Sea and Baltic, disguised under civilian markings. On October 24, twenty ships turned around rather than cross the quarantine line.

The Situation

Kennedy was humiliated by the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961, a CIA-backed attempt to overthrow Castro that collapsed within days. He had been in office less than a year and was seen by Khrushchev as young and inexperienced. He could not afford to appear weak again.

What Kennedy Wanted

  • Removal of Soviet missiles from Cuba without triggering nuclear war
  • To avoid a military invasion if at all possible
  • A public victory. He could not be seen backing down.
  • To maintain US nuclear advantage in the Western Hemisphere

Pressures Kennedy Faced

  • Military advisors including the Joint Chiefs pushed hard for immediate air strikes and invasion
  • Republican critics were already accusing him of being soft on Cuba
  • Congressional elections were weeks away
  • Any deal that looked like a concession could destroy his presidency
  • He was secretly managing severe back pain and taking multiple medications throughout the crisis
Age in 196268
In power since1953
Key vulnerabilityHardliners who saw him as too cautious

The Situation

Khrushchev faced pressure from hardliners within the Soviet military and Communist Party. The USSR was behind the United States in the nuclear arms race. Cuba offered a chance to close that gap and protect a new communist ally.

What Khrushchev Wanted

  • Protection of Cuba from a US invasion he believed was coming
  • Strategic parity, to counter US missiles in Turkey and Italy
  • A public win to demonstrate Soviet strength and resolve

Pressures Khrushchev Faced

  • Soviet military commanders in Cuba had more authority than Moscow realized and were prepared to act independently
  • Communist Party hardliners would use any retreat as evidence of weakness
  • He was ultimately removed from power in 1964, partly because of how the crisis ended
Age in 196236
In power since1959
Key vulnerabilityEntirely dependent on Soviet protection

The Situation

Castro had come to power in 1959 after overthrowing the US-backed Batista regime. The US had already tried to kill him multiple times and organized the Bay of Pigs invasion. He was genuinely convinced another US invasion was coming, and he was not wrong to think so.

What Castro Wanted

  • Soviet military protection against a US invasion
  • Recognition of Cuban sovereignty, the right to exist without US interference

Pressures Castro Faced

  • The deal was made between Kennedy and Khrushchev without his input
  • He was furious that Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles without consulting him
  • He urged Khrushchev to launch a nuclear first strike if the US invaded, a position Khrushchev ignored
  • The outcome left Cuba with only a weak US promise not to invade

Section 5  ·  October 27, 1962

300 Feet Underwater

Soviet submarine B-59 had been submerged for weeks. Its batteries were failing. Temperature inside had exceeded 100 degrees Fahrenheit in some compartments. Carbon dioxide levels were dangerously high. The crew had received no radio communications for days.

US destroyers had been dropping depth charges around the submarine. The Americans were signaling B-59 to surface, not trying to destroy it. But the crew did not know that. Captain Valentin Savitsky believed nuclear war had already begun above them.

Savitsky ordered the nuclear torpedo armed and prepared for launch. Under Soviet protocol, firing required authorization from three officers: the captain, the political officer, and the flotilla commander. The flotilla commander, Vasili Arkhipov, happened to be aboard B-59.

"We are going to blast them now! We will die, but we will sink them all. We will not become the shame of the fleet."
Captain Valentin Savitsky, B-59, October 27, 1962

Arkhipov refused to authorize the launch. He argued that the depth charges were signals, not attacks, and that surfacing to confirm orders was the right course of action. He convinced Savitsky to stand down. The torpedo was never launched.

Thomas Blanton of the National Security Archive later said: "A guy called Vasili Arkhipov saved the world."

Section 6  ·  Simulation

Build the Deal

It is the evening of October 27, 1962. Black Saturday is ending. Khrushchev has sent two letters with different demands. You are President Kennedy. What do you agree to?

The Soviet Demand, Part 1

Khrushchev's first letter offers a deal: the USSR will remove its missiles from Cuba if the United States publicly pledges never to invade Cuba. What do you do?

What Kennedy Actually Did

Kennedy accepted publicly. The US pledged not to invade Cuba and this was announced openly. It gave Khrushchev something he could show his own government as a win for Soviet diplomacy. Without it, Khrushchev would have had nothing to show for backing down.

The Soviet Demand, Part 2

Khrushchev's second letter raises the stakes: the USSR will only withdraw from Cuba if the United States removes its Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Your advisors are divided. What do you do?

What Kennedy Actually Did

Kennedy secretly agreed to remove the Jupiter missiles, conveying this through his brother Robert Kennedy in a private meeting with the Soviet ambassador. He made clear that if Khrushchev revealed the deal, the offer would be withdrawn.

The Jupiter missiles were quietly removed from Turkey six months later. The American public did not learn about this part of the deal until the 1980s, when declassified documents revealed it. The resolution was more mutual than Americans were told.

Your Verdict

Kennedy accepted the non-invasion pledge publicly and secretly agreed to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Khrushchev got both things he most wanted: Cuba protected and the Turkish missiles removed. Kennedy got the missiles out of Cuba and kept the Turkey deal secret.

Did Kennedy win the crisis? Did he deserve credit, blame, or both? Was the secret Turkey deal a reasonable compromise or a dangerous precedent? Could any leader have done better given the constraints they faced?

Section 7  ·  Context

The Bigger Picture

Connecting to Other Units

While Kennedy and Khrushchev stared each other down, the United States was not just a Cold War actor. It was a country in the middle of its own profound internal struggles. The same thirteen days looked very different depending on who you were and where you lived.

Civil Rights Movement

In October 1962, James Meredith had just enrolled at the University of Mississippi under federal escort, triggering riots that killed two people. The Birmingham Campaign was months away. Black Americans faced the prospect of nuclear war in a country that still denied them basic rights. Civil rights leaders continued their work even as the nation held its breath.

Vietnam, An Early Warning

In October 1962, the US had 11,000 military advisors in South Vietnam. Not yet a war officially, but heading toward one. Kennedy was simultaneously managing the missile crisis and increasing US involvement in Southeast Asia. The same Cold War logic that drove the standoff was pulling the US deeper into Vietnam.

The Nuclear Reality

Most Americans in 1962 lived with the daily awareness that nuclear war was possible. Schoolchildren practiced duck-and-cover drills. Cities had fallout shelter signs. The crisis made that abstract fear suddenly concrete, and confirmed that decisions made in secret by a handful of men could end civilization.

What We Did Not Know

For decades, Americans believed Kennedy had clearly won a confrontation where the Soviets blinked. The secret Jupiter deal, the near-launch on B-59, the unauthorized SAM that shot down the U-2. None of this was public. The full story emerged only through declassified documents and Soviet memoirs in the 1980s and 1990s. History often looks cleaner from a distance than it was in the moment.
